Action Plan:
1. Arrange same-day, face-to-face GP appointment in a Central London clinic for full neurological and otoscopic examination of left-sided hearing loss, facial/jaw numbness and intermittent tinnitus/dizziness. Admin team to contact patient; patient instructed to phone support line in 5 minutes to book convenient slot.
2. Discuss provisional diagnosis of Bell’s palsy; counsel that alternative causes (e.g., vestibular schwannoma, Ramsay Hunt, stroke) need exclusion. Reassure patient that immediate life-threatening pathology is unlikely.
3. Safety-net: advise patient to seek urgent care (call 999/A&E) if she develops facial weakness, limb weakness, speech or swallowing difficulties, new severe headache, ear pain, vesicular rash, or worsening dizziness.
4. Continue current intermittent intranasal spray (name, dose/frequency not documented) and OTC Rennie as required; no new drugs prescribed today.
5. Record latex allergy prominently in notes.
6. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Reason for visit: 3-week history of reduced hearing in left ear and constant numbness along left ear/jawline.  
• Associated symptoms: Intermittent left-sided tinnitus; occasional dizziness when tinnitus occurs.  
• Negatives: No ear pain, discharge, itching, fever, limb weakness, dysphagia, dysarthria, vision changes.  
• Past medical history: Nasal polyps; past episode labelled “labyrinthitis.”  
• Medications: Intermittent intranasal spray for nasal polyps (name/dose/frequency not documented); OTC antacid (Rennie).  
• Allergies: Latex.  
• Family history: Brother with neurofibromatosis.  
• Social: 40-year-old female jockey; lives with partner; no pets mentioned; no substance use discussed.  
• Patient anxiety about seriousness of symptoms expressed.

Objective:
• No physical examination performed on video call.  
• No vitals available.  
• No investigations performed to date.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Left-sided hearing loss with facial numbness  
   – Assessment / likely diagnosis: Bell’s palsy (idiopathic facial-nerve neuritis). DDx ranked “Medium” likelihood in DDx list.  
   – Differential diagnosis:  
     • Vestibular schwannoma (High) – unilateral sensorineural loss, tinnitus, facial numbness; family history of NF supports.  
     • Ramsay Hunt syndrome (Low-Medium) – unilateral symptoms but lacks pain/rash.  
     • Brainstem stroke, MS, other CPA tumours – less likely but considered.  
   – Investigations planned: Same-day in-person neurological & otoscopic examination; consider audiogram and MRI internal auditory meatus/CPA if exam suggests sensorineural loss or facial nerve involvement (to be arranged after GP review).  
   – Treatment planned: Pending exam findings. If Bell’s palsy confirmed, likely oral prednisolone within 72 h of onset (note onset 3 weeks—may be beyond window) and eye-protection advice; defer until exam.  
   – Relevant referrals: ENT or Neurology referral if suspicion of vestibular schwannoma or other pathology after initial GP assessment.

2. Patient anxiety regarding possible serious illness  
   – Assessment / likely diagnosis: Health-related anxiety secondary to above symptoms.  
   – Differential diagnosis: General situational anxiety.  
   – Management: Provided reassurance regarding low immediate risk; safety-net advice given; scheduled definitive in-person evaluation today.  
   – Referral: Consider mental-health support if anxiety persists after diagnostic clarification.

Quality checks:
• Missing but expected: Vitals, cranial-nerve exam, otoscopy, medication name/dose, substance use, menstrual/obstetric history.  
• Transcript/DDx conflicts: Doctor favoured Bell’s palsy; DDx lists vestibular schwannoma as higher likelihood – conflict noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear; minor pauses, no inaudible sections affecting data capture.
